result.target_topic: Holding company reliance on subsidiary payments
result.target_summary: Group Inc. is a holding company that depends on dividends, distributions, loans, and other payments from its subsidiaries to fund share repurchases, dividend payments, and debt obligations. Many subsidiaries are subject to laws restricting the flow of funds to the parent.

target_year_over_year_context.explanation: The 2023 disclosure gs_2023_1A_D049 covers two distinct aspects of holding company subsidiary restrictions: (1) the general dependency on subsidiary payments/loans and legal/regulatory restrictions on the flow of funds (matches gs_2024_1A_D046); and (2) specific restrictions on broker-dealer/bank subsidiaries regarding affiliate transactions, capital requirements, and fund usage, and the potential need for Group Inc. to provide additional funding (matches gs_2024_1A_D047). These are separated in 2024 into two distinct disclosures.

previous_disclosures.section: Liquidity > THE GOLDMAN SACHS GROUP, INC. AND SUBSIDIARIES
previous_disclosures.summary: As a holding company, Group Inc. depends on dividends, distributions, and loans from subsidiaries to fund its obligations, including debt and dividend payments. Many subsidiaries are subject to legal, regulatory, and capital restrictions that may block, reduce, or limit the flow of funds to Group Inc., particularly in times of stress, and may require Group Inc. to provide additional funding to subsidiaries.

comparisons.peer_topic: Legal entity structure and restrictions on intercompany fund transfers
comparisons.peer_summary: The parent company depends on dividends and loans from subsidiaries for liquidity but faces legal, regulatory, and contractual restrictions on transferring funds, including dividend limits, capital requirements, and resolution planning arrangements.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs (GS) and Bank of America (BAC) disclose that as holding companies, they depend on dividends, distributions, loans, and other payments from subsidiaries to fund obligations, including debt and dividend payments. Both also explicitly state that many of their subsidiaries, particularly broker-dealer and bank entities, are subject to laws and regulations that restrict these fund flows or allow regulators to block or reduce them. GS specifically mentions using these funds for share repurchases, while BAC specifies preferred and common stock dividends.

sentences.text: Group Inc. is a holding company and, therefore, depends on dividends, distributions, loans and other payments from its subsidiaries to fund share repurchases and dividend payments and to fund payments on its obligations, including debt obligations.

Many of our subsidiaries, including our broker-dealer and bank subsidiaries, are subject to laws that restrict dividend payments or authorize regulatory bodies to block or reduce the flow of funds from those subsidiaries to Group Inc.

The parent company depends on dividends, distributions, loans and other payments from our bank and nonbank subsidiaries to fund dividend payments on our preferred stock and common stock and to fund all payments on our other obligations, including debt obligations.

Many of our subsidiaries, including our bank and broker-dealer subsidiaries, are subject to laws that restrict dividend payments, or authorize regulatory bodies to block or reduce the flow of funds from those subsidiaries to the parent company or other subsidiaries.

comparisons.peer_summary: Citigroup Inc.'s liquidity depends on payments from subsidiaries, which may be restricted by capital adequacy rules, regulatory stress tests, or affiliate transaction limits for broker-dealer and bank subsidiaries.
comparisons.comparison: Citigroup (C) and Goldman Sachs (GS) both disclose that their liquidity and ability to satisfy debt and other obligations rely on interest, dividends, distributions, and other payments from subsidiaries. Both companies highlight that this reliance creates risk because their subsidiaries, including broker-dealer and bank units, face legal, regulatory, or contractual restrictions (such as capital adequacy rules or affiliate transaction limits) that may limit or block these payments.

sentences.text: Group Inc. is a holding company and, therefore, depends on dividends, distributions, loans and other payments from its subsidiaries to fund share repurchases and dividend payments and to fund payments on its obligations, including debt obligations.

Group Inc. is a holding company and its liquidity depends on payments and loans from its subsidiaries, many of which are subject to legal, regulatory and other restrictions on providing funds or assets to Group Inc.
As a holding company, Citigroup Inc. relies on interest, dividends, distributions and other payments from its subsidiaries to fund dividends as well as to satisfy its debt and other obligations.

Several of Citi's U.S. and non-U.S. subsidiaries are or may be subject to capital adequacy or other liquidity, regulatory or contractual restrictions on their ability to provide such payments, including any local regulatory stress test requirements and inter-affiliate arrangements entered into in connection with Citigroup Inc.'s resolution plan.

comparisons.peer_topic: Holding company structure and cash flow dependence
comparisons.peer_summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co. depends on subsidiary cash flows for payments and uses an intermediate holding company structure to manage capital and liquidity contributions.
comparisons.comparison: JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Goldman Sachs (GS) both identify themselves as holding companies that depend on the cash flows, payments, or loans from their subsidiaries to make payments on outstanding securities, debt, and other obligations. While GS broadly lists 'dividends, distributions, loans and other payments,' JPM specifically notes its dependence on cash flows to make payments on outstanding securities, and both highlight the structural reliance on subsidiary operations.

comparisons.peer_topic: Holding company structure and subsidiary payment restrictions
comparisons.peer_summary: As a holding company, the firm depends on subsidiary payments to fund obligations and dividends, but regulatory, tax, and legal restrictions, including ring-fencing measures, may limit or block these fund transfers.
comparisons.comparison: Morgan Stanley (MS) and Goldman Sachs (GS) both state that the parent holding company depends on dividends, distributions, loans, and other payments from subsidiaries to fund dividend payments and obligations, including debt. Both disclosures further explain that regulatory, legal, or tax restrictions may limit the ability to transfer funds freely, and specifically note that bank and broker-dealer subsidiaries are subject to laws that can block or reduce the flow of funds to the parent.

sentences.text: Group Inc. is a holding company and, therefore, depends on dividends, distributions, loans and other payments from its subsidiaries to fund share repurchases and dividend payments and to fund payments on its obligations, including debt obligations.

Many of our subsidiaries, including our broker-dealer and bank subsidiaries, are subject to laws that restrict dividend payments or authorize regulatory bodies to block or reduce the flow of funds from those subsidiaries to Group Inc.

The Parent Company has no business operations and depends on dividends, distributions, loans and other payments from its subsidiaries to fund dividend payments and to fund all payments on its obligations, including debt obligations.
Regulatory restrictions, tax restrictions or elections and other legal restrictions may limit our ability to transfer funds freely, either to or from our subsidiaries.
